name: Namibia
headline: Namibia has no data protection law in force and no shared patient record, so patients rely on a charter, ethics rules and the Constitution.

access.summary: The Ministry's Patient Charter promises you can obtain and inspect a copy of your health information, but no law in force gives an enforceable right. The 2022 Access to Information Act is still not in force.
detail: The Ministry of Health and Social Services Patient Charter says patients can expect "to obtain and inspect a copy of your health information". It is a statement of commitment, not a law, and it sets no deadline or fee rule.

The 2010 ethical guidelines of the Health Professions Councils tell health professionals to allow patients access to their medical records. Breaching them is a professional conduct matter, not a statutory right the patient can enforce in court.

The Access to Information Act 8 of 2022 would give a right to information held by public entities, which include state hospitals. In March 2026 the ICT minister halted recruitment of the Information Commissioner, and in May 2026 The Namibian reported the Act had yet to come into effect.
We found no national patient portal or app. Without a data protection law, there is no general right to a copy of personal data.

control.summary: The Patient Charter says health information will not be disclosed without consent, but no law gives patients sharing choices, an opt-out or an access log. Facilities hold the record and decide how it is used.
detail: The Patient Charter says personal health information "will be stored securely and not disclosed to others without your consent" and accessed only by those who need it for care. It also warns that records may be accessed for audit.

The professional ethical guidelines require a patient's permission before sharing information with spouses, partners or relatives, but allow disclosure for a "good and overriding reason" such as a public health emergency.

There is no shared national record, so there is no setting where a patient can choose who sees it or check who opened it. The 2026 Digital Health Policy says future systems will have privacy and consent mechanisms built in, which is a plan, not a rule in force.

privacy.summary: Namibia has no data protection law, regulator or breach notice rule in force; the Data Protection Bill was still being finalised in July 2026. Health data relies on the Constitution's privacy article and narrow rules such as a N$50,000 fine for disclosing STI status.
detail: Article 13 of the Constitution protects the privacy of homes, correspondence and communications, with exceptions in law for health, security and crime. It does not mention health records or personal data.

Section 35 of the Public and Environmental Health Act 2015 makes disclosing a person's STI status an offence, with a fine up to N$50,000 or five years in prison. In a declared public health emergency, section 30 lets authorised persons collect, use or disclose personal information.

In July 2026 the ICT minister said the Data Protection Bill and Cybercrime Bill were still being finalised. With no general health-sector rules, this scores the narrow sector laws, below the band for countries with a general law.

In August 2026 the government rejected a US health data and specimen-sharing proposal, saying it infringed the constitutional right to privacy. The Communications Act provisions on interception centres have been in force since January 2023. Namibia is outside the EU, so the EHDS does not apply.

commercial.summary: No law stops the sale or marketing use of health data. The opt-in rule for electronic marketing in the Electronic Transactions Act 2019 sits in Chapter 4, which the annotated text shows is still not in force.
detail: Section 36 of the Electronic Transactions Act 2019 would allow unsolicited commercial messages only with opt-in, require an opt-out in every message and set fines up to N$500,000. The annotated Act shows Chapter 4, which holds section 36, is not yet in force.

With no data protection law, there are no rules on data brokers, de-identified data sales or consumer health apps. A May 2026 opinion in The Namibian notes there is no data protection authority or uniform rule on data processing.
The Digital Health Policy plans a licensing and certification system for digital health platforms and providers. This is not yet in place.

journey.summary: The Ministry's own 2026 policy calls the digital health system siloed, with limited interoperability. An e-Health network reaches all hospitals and some health centres, and a national exchange (NAM-X) is planned, not running.
detail: The National Digital Health Policy 2026-2036 says the system is characterised by siloed solutions and limited interoperability. It says the National eHealth Strategy 2021-2025 was constrained, fragmented and largely donor-dependent.

At the February 2026 launch, the minister said an HIV system "may not connect with patient records or pharmaceutical supply systems", WHO Africa reported. The policy plans FHIR standards and exchange through a national platform, NAM-X.

In her May 2025 budget motivation, the health minister said all hospitals and 23 health centres had network infrastructure for the e-Health system. What the system records and how widely it is used was not verified.
DHIS2 has collected aggregate public health data since 2014. Medical aid claims run through NAMAF standards; the policy plans electronic claims alignment.

clinical.summary: A clinician cannot open one record that follows the patient across public and private care. The Ministry claims real-time record access at some connected facilities, but the scope of that access was not verified.
detail: In May 2025 the health minister told Parliament that five health centres and 18 clinics were operational on the expanded e-Health network, "ensuring real-time access to patient records". We could not verify what records clinicians see or whether they follow patients between facilities.
The minister said in February 2026 that poor system integration leads to missing records, repeated tests and delays in treatment, the Namibian Observer reported.
The Digital Health Policy aims to equip all health facilities with functional EMRs. There is no published emergency access rule for a shared record because no shared record exists.

research.summary: Health research goes through the Ministry's Biomedical Research Ethics Committee and Research Management Committee, and ethics rules require informed consent. There is no data protection law and no opt-out from secondary use of records.
detail: The Ministry runs a Biomedical Research Ethics Committee and a Research Management Committee, which review protocols under the Ministry's Guidelines on Clinical Trials and Research Management Policy, according to Health Research Web Africa.

The professional ethical guidelines require authorisation from relevant authorities, informed consent from participants and a right to withdraw at any time. They do not set rules for reuse of routine records without consent.

With no consent rule and no opt-out for secondary use, this starts at the base of the band. One safeguard class is documented (an ethics and approval body). Statutory secrecy covers only STI status, so we did not count it.

ai.summary: The medicines regulator says it does not currently regulate medical devices, so AI used in care has no device approval route. The 2026 Digital Health Policy only plans future AI guidelines.
detail: The Namibia Medicines Regulatory Council says it "does not currently regulate medical devices", except devices with an active pharmaceutical ingredient and Covid antigen tests. It says it is working on device guidelines.

The Digital Health Policy 2026-2036 commits to develop regulations, standards, ethical frameworks and guidelines for AI integration, and to coordinate AI programmes. No timeline is set in the text we read.
We found no national AI law and no binding guidance on clinical AI, human oversight or change control.

journeyNote: All hospitals have e-Health network links and DHIS2 gathers aggregate data, but the Ministry calls systems siloed. HIV, pharmacy and patient record systems do not connect, and the NAM-X exchange is planned.

laws.name: Namibian Constitution, Article 13
laws.what: Protects privacy of homes, correspondence and communications, with lawful exceptions including for health.

laws.name: Public and Environmental Health Act 1 of 2015
laws.what: Disease notification; STI status confidentiality with N$50,000 fine; emergency powers to collect and disclose personal information.

laws.name: Access to Information Act 8 of 2022
laws.what: Right to information held by public entities, including state hospitals; not yet in force.

laws.name: Electronic Transactions Act 4 of 2019
laws.what: Recognises electronic records; Chapter 4 marketing opt-in rule not yet in force.

laws.name: Medicines and Related Substances Control Act 13 of 2003
laws.what: Sets up the medicines regulator NMRC; medical devices are not currently regulated.

laws.name: Health Professions Act 16 of 2024
laws.what: Creates the Health Professions Council of Namibia to register and discipline health professionals; in force March 2025.

laws.name: Communications Act 8 of 2009, Part 6 of Chapter V
laws.what: Interception centres staffed by the intelligence service; in force from 1 January 2023.

news.headline: Minister says Data Protection Bill is ready to return to Cabinet
news.why: Patients still have no general data protection law or regulator.

news.why: Sets the plan for connected records and patient privacy rules.

news.why: Delays the law that could give access to records held by state hospitals.

news.headline: Government rejects US health data-sharing proposal, citing privacy and sovereignty
news.why: Shows the state treating patients' medical data as protected by the Constitution.
